label: dignity culture
source_text: [Vignoles et al. 2026, PSPB, citing Leung & Cohen 2011 for the tripartite distinction; a later paper's characterisation, not Leung & Cohen's words:] "In societies thought to promote a cultural logic of dignity (e.g., North American and Northwest European societies), individuals are presumed to have inherent, equal, and inalienable worth that is not easily lost through one's own or others' actions (Stewart, 1994). Accordingly, people living in these societies expect to behave according to their own internal standards, beliefs, and values, rather than external influences such as social condemnation or punishment (Ayers, 1984), and they expect legal systems to enforce lawful behavior, provide protection, and administer justice fairly and equally to all (A. Smith, 1976)."
description_draft: This means taking one's worth as inborn, equal to anyone's and beyond anyone's power to take away, shrugging off an insult, and answering to one's own standards, not to others' opinion.
nearest_existing: self_assured (sure of one's own worth, taking criticism without feeling smaller: a temperament of confidence; this pole is a theory of where worth comes from, inborn and equal and untakeable, and what follows for insults and conduct); thick_skinned carries the shrug alone; principled and independent carry the own-standards clause alone; dignified shares the word but is bearing and composure, not the source of worth.
notes: Second source, Cross et al. (2014), PSPB, Bilkent OA copy (repository.bilkent.edu.tr/bitstreams/eac3c5f9-ca30-4697-9e39-eefa8435acfb/download), paraphrasing: 'in nonhonor (or dignity) cultures, the individual is assumed to have inherent worth that is equal to every other person's worth and that cannot be taken away by others (Leung & Cohen, 2011). Internal standards and goals rather than social expectations are the ideal motivators of good behavior.' Source words to draft: 'inherent, equal, and inalienable worth' -> 'inborn, equal to anyone's'; 'cannot be taken away by others' -> 'beyond anyone's power to take away'; 'insults can be ignored' (the approved concept text) -> 'shrugging off an insult'; 'their own internal standards ... rather than external influences such as social condemnation' -> 'answering to one's own standards, not to others' opinion'. Left out for length: the expectation that the law, not oneself, punishes wrongs (Vignoles; Kent thesis), which is the behavioural counterpart of not answering an insult; a reviewer may prefer it to the shrug. Strength: the sources are unhedged except 'not easily lost', which the draft renders as the stronger 'beyond anyone's power to take away' following Cross et al.'s 'cannot be taken away'; flag if the milder form is wanted. Label kept out of the description. The dignity and face texts are paraphrases by later papers citing Leung & Cohen, not quotations: see the fetch record. Leung & Cohen (2011), JPSP 100(3), 507-526, doi 10.1037/a0022151, is paywalled at APA and no open copy could be read: OpenAlex lists two repository copies, SMU InK (ink.library.smu.edu.sg/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2282&context=soss_research), which served an Incapsula bot-check page to both WebFetch and curl, and DigitalGeorgetown (hdl 10822/1040467), which is 410 Gone; web.archive.org is not reachable from this tool; Semantic Scholar answered 429 on every call; scholar.archive.org and archive.org's search were rate-limited; CORE 403; PubMed served only a cookie page. (2014, PSPB, Bilkent OA copy) and Vignoles et al. (2026, PSPB, PMC13022031) paraphrase without quotation marks. set_review: Honor / dignity / face triangle. One grain: each draft says what one's worth is and where it comes from, and the test case is the same, an insult or a misstep. Honor: worth is a standing claimed before others and paid by them; an unanswered insult removes it and only an answer restores it. Dignity: worth is inborn, equal and untakeable; the insult is shrugged off and one's own standards govern. Face: worth is standing granted by others for filling one's place and lost at a misstep; kept by claiming nothing beyond one's due, harmony, rank, and saving others' face. Pairwise contrasts are all live: honor vs dignity is conferred vs inherent and answer vs shrug; honor vs face is two kinds of conferred worth, claimed and defended against the one who withholds it versus granted for fitting one's place and kept by restraint; dignity vs face is inherent vs conferred and own standards vs the order's expectations. Geometry caveat: on the inherent/conferred axis dignity stands alone and honor and face sit together (the word 'standing' appears in both, deliberately), so the honor-face side may come out shorter than the other two unless the claim/defer contrast carries; the approved concept text draws the same picture. Strength mirrors the sources: honor's 'does not in fact have honor' is the firmest and the honor draft the most forceful ('only answering it wins it back'); dignity and face are stated plainly without hedges, as Vignoles et al. and Cross et al. state them ('not easily lost' sharpened to 'beyond anyone's power to take away', flagged in notes). Shape: all three open 'This means taking/treating one's worth as ...', 29-32 words, a colon or comma then two or three particulars. Provenance caveat for the reviewer: only the honor sentence is Leung & Cohen verbatim (p. 509, via De Leersnyder et al. 2013); dignity and face rest on open-access later papers' characterisations citing Leung & Cohen plus the approved concept text, since no open copy of the article could be read. Two wording flags: 'shrugging off an insult' (dignity) borders on thick_skinned, and 'saving others' face' (face) uses the label word, kept because it is the persona's own idiom; a reviewer may swap it for 'sparing others' standing'.

label: face culture

Face is easily lost if norms are violated or expectations are unmet (Hamamura et al., 2009). Hence, individuals adopt actions (e.g., cooperation, self-restraint, conformity) to protect their own and close others' face, and concerns for humility, ingroup harmony, and hierarchy are widespread (Kim & Cohen, 2010)."

label: fear-prone
source_text: [Jayson Georges, HonorShame.com, 'Understanding Guilt, Shame, and Fear Cultures', 2014-11-05, bylined HonorShame:] fear-power cultures are "animistic contexts (typically tribal), where people afraid of evil and harm pursue power over the spirit world through magical rituals." [Georges, 'The Meaning of Fear-Power: 3 Options', honorshame.com/meaning-fear-power/, 2018-05-30, the religious and the political sense:] "People live in fear of unseen forces such as mana, curses, witches, and ancestors. Consequently, they seek spiritual power over those forces through ritual practices." "Power is the ability to exercise control over other people. Leaders instill a sense of fear by making threats. People submit to leaders because they fear the negative repercussions of appearing disrespectful."
description_draft: This means being kept in line by fear of those who can punish: submitting to the strong, appeasing spirits and ancestors, and seeking in rites the power that keeps harm away.
nearest_existing: preconventional_kohlberg (right is what avoids punishment or pays, judged by the power of whoever lays down the rule: a basis of moral judgment that also covers reward and exchange; this pole is the sanction that keeps one in line, retribution by a power human or unseen, with appeasement and power-seeking as the remedy); superstitious is omens and luck with no punisher behind them, obedient and submissive are compliance with authority as such, cowardly is letting fear decide in a danger, and anxious / paranoid / timid / panicky are states of feeling, which the approved concept text says this pole must not be.
notes: The same 2014 post defines the other two types: guilt-innocence cultures are 'individualistic societies (mostly Western), where people who break the laws are guilty and seek justice or forgiveness to rectify a wrong'; shame-honor cultures are 'collectivistic cultures (common in the East), where people are shamed for not fulfilling group expectations and seek to restore their honor before the community'. HonorShame.com was founded by Georges in 2013 and became the Honor-Shame Network's platform in 2016 (its About page), so the 2014 post is his own; the 2018 post is bylined 'HonorShame (Jason)'. Which author: Georges for this corner (Benedict has no fear culture); Roland Muller, Honor and Shame: Unlocking the Door (2000), could not be read: rmuller.com/shame.html and rmuller.com/mmc.html carry only the book blurb and the chapter list (ch. 13 'Guilt-Based Worldviews', ch. 15 'Fear-Based Worldviews', ch. 16 'Shame-Based Worldviews'), with no excerpt; the Smashwords page (books/view/307859) and its sample reader returned only site navigation to this tool; the only verbatim sentence about Muller found is Georges's, 'Roland Muller's book Honor & Shame: Unlocking the Door (2001) expanded and popularized the notion guilt, shame, and fear cultures for Christian ministry' (honorshame.com/model-guilt-shame-fear/, 2018-05-24). The 3D Gospel's own pages on honorshame.com (3dgospel, 3d-gospel-new-e-book, the-3d-gospel) and theculturetest.com carry only blurbs; the Culture Test discussion-guide PDF has its text in image streams. Source words to draft: 'afraid of evil and harm' and 'fear of unseen forces' and 'fear the negative repercussions' -> 'kept in line by fear of those who can punish' (the approved concept text: 'the power of those who can punish (authorities, spirits, fate)'); 'People submit to leaders' -> 'submitting to the strong'; 'curses, witches, and ancestors' and 'the spirit world' -> 'appeasing spirits and ancestors'; 'pursue power over the spirit world through magical rituals' and 'seek spiritual power ... through ritual practices' -> 'seeking in rites the power that keeps harm away'. Not used: Georges's 'psychological' sense of fear-power (anxiety), because the approved concept text requires a control logic, not anxiety, or the pole collapses onto anxious / paranoid / the prey role; the draft's content is the sanction and the remedies, not a feeling. 'Fate' from the concept text is not in Georges and is left out. 'can' in 'those who can punish' is capability, not a hedge. Strength: the sources are unhedged ('live in fear', 'submit'); the draft matches. Wikipedia's 'Guilt-shame-fear spectrum of cultures' lead ('control is kept by the fear of retribution') and KnowledgeWorkx's 'Three Colors of Worldview' (Blankenburgh, 2020: people 'assess where they fit into the pecking order ... and behave accordingly ... align themselves with the right people to gain more power') agree but quote no author, so they are cross-checks only.
set_review: Guilt / shame / fear triangle. One grain: each draft names the sanction that keeps the persona in line and then the same test case, how a fault feels and what one does about it. Guilt: one's own conscience and picture of oneself; the misdeed gnaws even unseen; confession relieves. Shame: others' eyes; ridicule or rejection, even imagined, stings; a fault that never gets out does not trouble; confession brings no relief. Fear: the power that punishes; one submits to the strong, appeases spirits and ancestors, and seeks power over harm in rites. Pairwise contrasts: guilt vs shame is Benedict's own, an audience needed or not and confession a relief or a danger; shame vs fear is others' criticism versus retribution and harm, with concealment versus appeasement as the remedy; guilt vs fear is an inner standard versus an outer power, confession versus appeasement. The three share the opener 'This means being kept in line by ...', chosen so the grain is unmistakable (what regulates conduct, as the approved concept text puts it); the cost is that the shared phrase may pull the three description embeddings together, and each corner's content after the colon is distinct enough that the opener can be varied if the reviewer prefers. Caveats: the fear corner comes from a different author and register (Georges's missiology, written about societies: 'animistic contexts (typically tribal)') than Benedict's two, and is individualised here per the queue, so its particulars (spirits, ancestors, rites) make it read as a tribal-religious persona more than the other two read as any culture; the concept text's 'authorities' is carried by 'the strong' and 'fate' is left out. Strength: Benedict is strong ('a potent sanction', 'does not experience relief') and Georges strong ('live in fear'); the drafts carry no hedges beyond Benedict's own, which the guilt and shame notes record ('may actually be relieved' -> 'brings relief'; 'need not be troubled' -> 'untroubled'). Shape: 30-31 words each, opener, colon, three particulars. Against the corpus: guilt is not remorseful (after-the-harm repair toward the injured) or conscientious (diligence); shame is not self_conscious (being looked at as such) or reserved; fear is not anxious or cowardly; the one real neighbour is preconventional_kohlberg for the fear corner, noted on the entry.

label: guilt-prone
source_text: [Benedict 1946, ch. 10, p. 223:] "True shame cultures rely on external sanctions for good behavior, not, as true guilt cultures do, on an internalized conviction of sin. Shame is a reaction to other people's criticism. A man is shamed either by being openly ridiculed and rejected or by fantasying to himself that he has been made ridiculous. In either case it is a potent sanction. But it requires an audience or at least a man's fantasy of an audience. Guilt does not. In a nation where honor means living up to one's own picture of oneself, a man may suffer from guilt though no man knows of his misdeed and a man's feeling of guilt may actually be relieved by confessing his sin."
description_draft: This means being kept in line by one's own conscience and one's own picture of oneself: a misdeed gnaws at one though nobody knows of it, and confessing it brings relief.
nearest_existing: remorseful (owning the harm done, apologizing, wanting to make it right: the response after a harm, turned toward the injured party; this pole is the sanction that keeps one in line beforehand and bites with no witness, relieved by confession); self_blaming is attribution of fault, moral is the pull of right and wrong, conscientious is diligence, which the approved concept text says this pole is not; judge test: would the persona be troubled by a wrong nobody will ever know of?
notes: Which author: Benedict, for guilt and shame. Source words to draft: 'an internalized conviction of sin' -> 'one's own conscience'; 'honor means living up to one's own picture of oneself' -> 'one's own picture of oneself'; 'may suffer from guilt though no man knows of his misdeed' -> 'a misdeed gnaws at one though nobody knows of it'; 'may actually be relieved by confessing his sin' -> 'confessing it brings relief'. Hedges: Benedict's 'may suffer' and 'may actually be relieved' are possibility stated for contrast with shame (where confession brings no relief), not psychometric softening; rendered as plain statements, flagged here in case the reviewer wants 'can bring relief'. 'Sin' rendered as 'misdeed' (Benedict's own word two clauses earlier) to keep the pole secular. The preceding sentences, not quoted, say the same of confession: 'This device of confession is used in our secular therapy and by many religious groups which have otherwise little in common. We know it brings relief.' Source: Ruth Benedict, The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), chapter 10, 'The Dilemma of Virtue'; read from the OCR text layer of the Internet Archive item in.ernet.dli.2015.80008 (Digital Library of India scan, 1947 printing per the item metadata), fetched by curl and grepped in memory. The OCR page marker '223' immediately follows the passage; the passage is the one standardly cited to p. 223 of the 1946 Houghton Mifflin edition (a second fetch to check the marker convention was rate-limited by archive.org, so 'p. 223' rests on the marker and the standard citation). OCR normalisation in source_text: line-end hyphens joined ('crit- icism', 're- quires', 'audi- ence', 'feel- ing', 'expia- tion'), curly quotes straightened; the OCR has 'httle' for 'little' in a sentence just before the quoted stretch, not quoted. The book is in copyright in the US, so this scan is the open copy the packet allows; Wikipedia's articles on the book and on the guilt-shame-fear spectrum carry no Benedict quotation, only the lead definitions (guilt society: 'control is maintained by creating and continually reinforcing the feeling of guilt (and the expectation of punishment now or in the afterlife) for certain condemned behaviors'; shame society: 'the means of control is the inculcation of shame and the complementary threat of ostracism'; fear society: 'control is kept by the fear of retribution'), used as a cross-check only.

A man is shamed either by being openly ridiculed and rejected or by fantasying to himself that he has been made ridiculous.
